IntroductionModel collaboration emerges as the foundation of systemlevel intelligence in the era of Agentic AI (Acharya et al., 2025). Recent advances in multi-agent systems (MAS) (Wu et al., 2024;Hu et al., 2025) have catalyzed a paradigm shift from solitary, model-centric reasoning into a collabora-tive endeavor among multiple interacting models. Among these, large language model (LLM)-based MAS has been adopted across various downstream applications, including cooperative math and science reasoning (Pezeshkpour et al., 2024;Zhou et al., 2025), automated code generation (Yang et al., 2024b;Ding et al., 2025), and open-domain question answering (Jin et al., 2025;Li et al., 2025c;2026). Within LLM-based MAS, natural language or text generally serves as the lingua franca -the common medium that carries each agent's internal thoughts and enables communication across different agents (Guo et al., 2024).Beyond explicit text, several studies have explored the use of LLMs' continuous latent space as a new form of "model language," (Chen et al., 2025b) by either (i) leveraging hidden representations within transformers to enable single model's internal latent chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning (Hao et al., 2024;Zheng et al., 2025;Zhang et al., 2025), or (ii) employing KV caches or layer embeddings for information exchange across two models (Liu et al., 2024;Fu et al., 2025). However, a comprehensive model collaboration framework unifying both latent reasoning and latent communication remains unexplored. Moving one step forward, we aim to investigate:
Can MAS achieve pure latent collaboration?To address this question, we introduce LatentMAS, an endto-end collaborative framework that operates entirely within the continuous latent space. Our core design integrates both internal latent thoughts generation and cross-agent latent working memory transfer. Inside each agent, reasoning unfolds through auto-regressive generation of last-layer hidden representations, capturing the model's ongoing internal thoughts without explicit decoding. Across agents, information is exchanged via shared latent working memory stored in layer-wise KV caches, capturing both the input context and newly generated latent thoughts. Overall, LatentMAS is completely training-free, enabling all agents to think and interact purely through their internal latent representations.Building on this framework design, LatentMAS is grounded on three foundational principles, which are substantiated through comprehensive theoretical and empirical analyses:• Reasoning Expressiveness: Hidden representations naturally encode model continuous thoughts, making each latent step more expressive than discrete tokens and capable of conveying richer semantic information.• Communication Fidelity: Latent working memory preserves input representations and latent thoughts, enabling lossless information transfer across agents.• Collaboration Complexity: LatentMAS exhibits higher collaborative expressiveness than text-based MAS with substantially lower inference complexity.The first two principles jointly underscore the advantage of LatentMAS by enabling richer latent reasoning and lossless latent communication. The last principle characterizes how latent collaboration reshapes the efficiency-expressiveness tradeoff, illustrating that LatentMAS enables scalable multiagent coordination with reduced computational overhead.To empirically assess the efficacy of LatentMAS, we conduct comprehensive evaluations on 9 benchmarks spanning math and science reasoning, commonsense understanding, and code generation (Figure 1). Across both sequential and hierarchical MAS settings, and over five different backbone models spanning the Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025) and Llama3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024) families, LatentMAS consistently outperforms advanced single-model and text-based MAS baselines by (i) improving accuracy by up to 14.6%, (ii) reducing output token usage by 70.8%-83.7%, and (iii) delivering 4×-4.3× faster end-to-end inference. These results demonstrate that latent collaboration not only enhances system-level reasoning quality but also provides consistent efficiency gains without any additional training. Further detailed analyses of latent thought expressiveness, workingmemory transfer, and input-output alignment confirm that LatentMAS enables semantically meaningful, lossless, and stable collaboration entirely in latent space.
Preliminary and NotationsAuto-regressive Generation in Transformer. Let f θ (•) denotes the function computed by a standard Transformer model (Vaswani et al., 2017), parameterized by θ. Given an input sequence x = (x 1 , x 2 , . . . , x T ), the transformer f θ (•) first encodes each token via its input embedding layer W in to obtain token embeddings up to step t, i.e., E = [e 1 , e 2 , . . . , e t ] ∈ R t×d h , where d h is the model's hidden dimension. The input token embeddings E then successively process through L transformer layers in the forward pass through the model's residual stream, yielding the finallayer hidden representations H = [h 1 , h 2 , . . . , h t ] ∈ R t×d h . For next token generation, the model computes:f θ (x t+1 | x ≤t ) = softmax(h t W out ),(1)where W out denotes the language model head that maps the hidden representation to the vocabulary space. Each token is generated in an auto-regressive manner and appended to the input sequence. For latent generation, the model performs auto-regression over hidden representations instead of tokens, bypassing explicit decoding (Hao et al., 2024).
KV Cache as Working Memory.In decoder-only Transformers, the Key-Value (KV) cache functions as a dynamic working memory during auto-regressive generation, storing intermediate representations from previous decoding steps to avoid redundant computation. Specifically, given the input embeddings E, each transformer layer projects them through projection matrices W Q , W K , W V to obtain Q, K, V . When the next token at step t + 1 is generated, the model appends its embedding to the input sequence and updates the cache (K cache , V cache ) as:K cache ← [K ≤t ; K t+1 ], V cache ← [V ≤t ; V t+1 ], (2)where K ≤t , V ≤t are accumulated key/value matrices from all previous steps and K t+1 , V t+1 are new key/value vectors computed from the current token's hidden state. This accumulative property enables the KV cache to maintain a growing working memory of model internal representations. 
LLM-based MAS Setting.We consider a multi-agent system S composed of N agents, denoted as A = {A 1 , A 2 , . . . , A N }, where each agent A i is an LLM corresponding to f θi above. At inference time, an input question q is provided to the system S, which orchestrates interactions among agents to collaboratively produce a final answer a corresponding to q. As MAS design paradigms are not definitive in general and often vary across downstream tasks (Tran et al., 2025;Cemri et al., 2025), we do not restrict our latent collaboration design to any particular architecture. Instead, we adopt two most commonly used MAS settings (sequential and hierarchical) as the bases to experimentally evaluate our method. Figure 2 illustrates the two MAS architecture settings. In the sequential MAS, we adopt a chain-of-agents design (Zhang et al., 2024b;Zhao et al., 2026) comprising four LLM agents: planner, critic, refiner, and solver. These agents assume complementary reasoning roles and are organized in a sequential pipeline, where the CoT output of each agent with the question q serves as the input to the next agent. In the hierarchical MAS, we adopt a domain-specialized design (Zhuge et al., 2024;Zhao et al., 2025). Multiple LLM agents, including code, math, and science agents, operate as different domain experts. Each agent independently reasons over the question q from its disciplinary perspective.A summarizer agent then receives all intermediate responses along with the question q and performs hierarchical aggregation to synthesize and refine the final answer.
LatentMASWe introduce LatentMAS, an end-to-end latent collaboration framework that all agents reason and communicate entirely within the latent space. As illustrated in Figure 3, our method enables LLM agents to (i) auto-regressively generate expressive latent thoughts (Section 3.1), (ii) transfer latent working memory across agents with lossless communication fidelity (Section 3.2), and (iii) achieve lower inference complexity than text-based MAS while supporting a higher degree of model coordination (Section 3.3).
Method Roadmap.In the following sub-sections, we present the complete pipeline of LatentMAS, detailing each component and interleaving theoretical analyses to justify the corresponding design principles.
Auto-regressive Latent Thoughts GenerationWe first describe how each LLM agent performs latent reasoning through its layer-wise hidden states. Instead of decoding explicit tokens, reasoning unfolds directly within the agent by auto-regressively appending hidden representations from the final model layer.Given the input embeddings E = [e 1 , e 2 , . . . , e t ] containing the information from the question q and each agent's instruction prompt, each LLM agent A i ∈ A passes E through L transformer layers to compute the last-layer hidden representation h t at current step t. Then, we insert h t as the input embedding for the next step t + 1, replacing the original decoding and next-token embedding processes used in standard token generation. We auto-regressively repeat the process for m latent steps, yielding a sequence of newly generated last-layer hidden states H = [h t+1 , h t+2 , . . . , h t+m ].We define the continuous output representations H as the latent thoughts generated by A i .
Input-Output Distribution Alignment.Since the newly generated H form a sequence of dense, high-level representations, directly inserting them into shallow layers as input embeddings may lead to out-of-distribution activations (Meegahapola et al., 2019;Zhou et al., 2019) , as these hidden states differ from the statistical patterns of learned token embeddings. To mitigate this in a training-free manner, we propose a linear alignment operator that maps last-layer hidden states back to the valid input embeddings. Specifically, given W in , W out as the input and output embedding layers of A i , we seek a projection matrix W a ∈ R d h ×d h that maps each output vector h ∈ H to a new input vector e to align with valid input space defined by W in :e = hW a , where W a ≈ W † out W in .(3)Here, W † out is the pseudo-inverse (Hoerl & Kennard, 1970) of W out (in Appendix A, we provide a detailed theoretical justification for the effectiveness of W a in the input-output alignment process, followed by a formal derivation of W a ).We then append the aligned vector e into the input sequence for auto-regressive latent generation. Note that W a is a small projection matrix of size d h × d h (e.g., d h =1024 for Qwen3-0.6B) and is computed once and reused in all subsequent latent steps. This design makes the alignment computationally negligible while maintaining distributional consistency between latent and discrete representations.Expressiveness on Continuous Latent Thoughts. With the mechanism of latent thought generation established within each agent, we next provide a theoretical analysis to quantify its representational advantage over conventional discrete token generation. The following theorem formalizes that latent thoughts, which inherently preserve richer semantic structures, achieve substantially higher expressive capacity than discrete text-based reasoning.Theorem 3.1 (Expressiveness of Latent Thoughts). Under the Linear Representation Hypothesis on h (stated in Assumption B.1), if the sequence of all latent thoughts with length m can be expressed losslessly through corresponding text-based reasoning, then the length of text (in tokens) needs to be at least Ω d h m/ log |V| , where |V| > 1 denotes the vocabulary size. Remark 3.2. Theorem 3.1 suggests that latent thoughts generation can be O d h / log |V| times more efficient than text-based reasoning. In addition, the expressiveness scales linearly with d h , implying that larger models inherently exhibits greater latent reasoning capacity.As an illustration to Remark 3.2, for Qwen3-4B / 8B / 14B models (Yang et al., 2025), latent thoughts generation can be 235.7 / 377.1 / 471.4 times more efficient than text-based reasoning. The full proof of Theorem 3.1 is provided in Appendix B.1. Beyond reasoning within individual agents, collaboration in LatentMAS further relies on how these agents exchange latent information, which we detail next.
Thoughts Transfer via Latent Working MemoryIn text-based MAS, after one LLM agent completes its generation, the natural language output is directly appended to the input sequence of the next agent. However, since each agent in LatentMAS performs hidden-state generation without explicit text outputs, we design a new latent working memory transfer mechanism to ensure lossless information preservation and exchange.For clarity, we describe the memory transfer mechanism using the first two consecutive LLM agents A 1 , A 2 ∈ A.As shown in Figure 3, agent A 1 first performs m latent steps of generation (Section 3.1). After completing these steps, we extract the KV-caches from all L transformer layers of A 1 once and collect the latent working memory of A 1 as:M A1 = K (l) A1,cache , V(l)A1,cache l = 1, 2, . . . , L , with K (l) A1,cache = [K (l) A1,1 , . . . , K (l) A1,t+m ], and V (l) A1,cache = [V (l) A1,1 , . . . , V (l) A1,t+m ].(4) Here K (l) A1,cache and V (l)A1,cache are accumulated key and value matrices at the l-th layer. Unlike direct cache-sharing methods that exchange information mainly on prefilled input context across models, the collection of layer-wise caches in M A1 encapsulates both the initial input context and the newly generated latent thoughts of agent A 1 .Next, the successive agent A 2 integrates the working memory M A1 from agent A 1 . Before A 2 generates latent thoughts (i.e., last-layer hidden states), we perform layerwise concatenation to update its KV cache by prepending each K(l) A1,cache and V (l) A1,cache to existing K (l) A2,cache and V (l)A2,cache . By doing so, the new latent thoughts generation in A 2 is conditioned on both the working memory of A 1 and its own internal representations.
Lossless Information Transfer.The latent working memory transfer mechanism ensures that each succeeding agent in LatentMAS seamlessly receives its predecessor's complete output without re-encoding. In the following theorem, we further formalize this property to demonstrate that latent working memory transfer guarantees information fidelity equivalent to explicit input exchange.
Theorem 3.3 (Information Preservation via Latent Working Memory).In both latent and text-based reasoning, the outputs of an agent when receiving latent working memory from preceding agents are equivalent to those obtained when directly inputting the preceding agents' outputs.Full proof of Theorem 3.3 is provided in B.2. With lossless information preservation, we transfer latent working memory in KV rather than directly transmitting hidden states to avoid redundant recomputation for the successive agent.
End-to-End Pipeline with Complexity AnalysesFor the remaining agents in LatentMAS, we follow the same latent thoughts generation and working memory transfer mechanism described above. Specifically, agent A 3 inherits the working memory M A2 from the preceding agent A 2 , performs auto-regressive last-layer hidden state generation, and subsequently transmits its updated latent working memory M A3 to the next agent. This process continues across all agents in LatentMAS, with only the last agent decoding the final answer in texts. In the following theorem, we theoretically analyze the overall complexity of LatentMAS.
Theorem 3.4 (LatentMAS Complexity).The time complexity for each agent of LatentMAS is O (d 2 h m + d h m 2 + d h tm)L , where t is the input length of this agent, and m is the length of latent thoughts. In contrast, assuming Theorem 3.1, the time complexity for each agent of the vanilla text-based MAS needs to be O d3 h m 1 log |V| + d 3 h m 2 1 log 2 |V| + d 2 h tm 1 log |V| L + d 2 h |V|m 1 log |V|to achieve the same expressiveness.The full proof of Theorem 3.4 is provided in B.3. It is worth noting that LatentMAS is agnostic to specific model collaboration strategies and can be seamlessly applied to sequential, hierarchical, or other advanced MAS designs.
Empirical EvaluationsTasks and Datasets. We conduct comprehensive evaluations of LatentMAS across 9 benchmarks spanning both general-purpose and reasoning-intensive tasks: (i) Math & Science Reasoning, including GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), AIME24 (Maxwell-Jia, 2024), AIME25 (math ai, 2025), GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2023), and MedQA (Yang et al., 2024a); (ii) Commonsense Reasoning, including ARC-Easy (Clark et al., 2018b) and ARC-Challenge (Clark et al., 2018a); and (iii) Code Generation, including MBPP-Plus (Liu et al., 2023) and HumanEval-Plus (Liu et al., 2023). Additional benchmark details are provided in Appendix C.1.

Main ResultsTables 1, 2, and 3 report the overall performance of Latent-MAS across 9 general and reasoning-intensive benchmarks built from 5 different scales of LLM backbones. To thoroughly examine collaboration behaviors during inference, we evaluate each method from three complementary perspectives: (i) task accuracy, (ii) system throughput (total output tokens), and (iii) end-to-end inference speed. Across all tasks, LatentMAS consistently improves over the singlemodel baseline by an average of 14.6% and 13.3% under the sequential and hierarchical settings, respectively, and further yields gains of 2.8% and 4.6% over text-based MAS. Under identical MAS architectures, LatentMAS provides 4× and 4.3× faster inference speed on average compared with sequential and hierarchical text-based MAS. Additionally, as the agents' collaboration occurs entirely in latent space, LatentMAS reduces token usage by 70.8% and 83.7% relative to sequential and hierarchical TextMAS. We leave additional results on Llama backbones in Appendix D.2. End-to-end Inference Speed. As established earlier in Theorem 3.1, LatentMAS can achieve orders-of-magnitude higher expressiveness, thereby enabling more efficient inference than text-based MAS. We further empirically validate this advantage through comparisons with TextMAS. As shown in Figure 4 and 10 (left), even after accelerating the TextMAS baselines using the vLLM service, LatentMAS still achieves a 2.6×-7× speedup over the vLLM-optimized TextMAS. This improvement stems from the substantially reduced number of latent steps required for latent thoughts generation compared with the much larger decoding steps needed for per-token text generation. With fewer than 50 latent steps, LatentMAS attains comparable or even higher performance on reasoning-intensive tasks such as AIME 24/25, whereas TextMAS typically requires more than 20K output tokens to complete full text-based CoT trajectories.Token Throughput. In addition, as illustrated in Figure 4 and 10 (right), LatentMAS reduces token usage by 59.4%-87.9% compared with TextMAS, as agents in LatentMAS communicate by directly transferring latent working memory into another agent's internal layers rather than relying on the text medium. LatentMAS also achieves 15.0%-60.3% lower token usage than single agents. Compared with singlemodel reasoning, LatentMAS distributes the input question across collaborating agents, greatly reducing the burden on the final agent, which primarily aggregates preceding latent thoughts and decodes the final answer using only a small number of tokens. As a result, the entire system generates fewer output tokens while still achieving higher accuracy.

Optimal Latent Step Depth.To understand how many latent steps are needed for optimal performance in Latent-MAS, we analyze the effect of increasing latent step depth across three downstream tasks. As shown in Figure 8, increasing the number of latent steps generally improves downstream performance, indicating that additional latent thoughts enhance collaborative expressiveness. Across the three tasks on Qwen3-14B, we find that accuracy steadily rises and peaks around 40-80 steps. Beyond this range, performance plateaus or declines, suggesting that excessive latent thought generation may introduce redundant or less useful information. Based on this observation, we adopt a moderate latent step budget within this range in practice, as it consistently provides the best accuracy-efficiency tradeoff without requiring any task-specific training procedures.

We leave implementation details on how to converse to the debug mode in LatentMAS, together with additional detailed analyses and case studies, to Appendix E,F, and J.
Related WorkLLM-based Multi-agent Systems. Recent studies in Agentic AI have extended classical multi-agent systems (Hong et al., 2023;Park et al., 2023a;Yang et al., 2024c) grounded in traditional reinforcement learning and policy coordination, to modern LLM settings (Li et al., 2025b;Tan et al., 2025), enabling models to operate as autonomous agents that collaborate in reasoning, planning, and problemsolving (Tao et al., 2024;Wang et al., 2025c;Zhao et al., 2025). Early methods (Yao et al., 2022;Wu et al., 2024;Li et al., 2023) coordinate multiple LLMs through explicit dialogue and role assignment. Additional methods introduce structured communication protocols to enhance cooperation efficiency (Ye et al., 2025a) and emergent specialization (Mieczkowski et al., 2025;Huang et al., 2026) among agents. Building upon these advanced text-MAS methods, our work aims to construct a multi-agent collaboration system entirely in latent space, treating agents as tightly integrated components to achieve more expressive and efficient coordination.
Model Collaboration in Latent Space.Recent studies on model collaboration (Tran et al., 2025) have gradually shifted from text-level coordination toward interaction directly in latent representations. Instead of exchanging information through texts, these works (Coda-Forno et al., 2025;Ye et al., 2025a;Fu et al., 2025;Zheng et al., 2025) enable models to communicate through model internal states such as hidden representations (Coda-Forno et al., 2025) for efficiency (Kong et al., 2026). Most existing methods rely on auxiliary alignment mechanisms and typically require additional training to facilitate effective cross-model communication. On the other hand, LatentMAS is a training-free latent multi-agent system in which each agent reasons and communicates via native latent representations.We leave additional related works on latent reasoning and agent collaboration in Appendix H.
ConclusionWe introduce LatentMAS, a training-free framework that enables multi-agent systems to collaborate entirely within latent space. Our framework enables latent auto-regressive reasoning with a lossless latent working-memory transfer mechanism. Theoretical analyses and empirical evaluations across diverse reasoning and generation benchmarks demonstrate that LatentMAS consistently improves accuracy performance, token usage, and decoding speed over strong single-model and text-based MAS baselines. Evaluation DetailsWe introduce all datasets used in our experiments as follows:Math & Science Reasoning.• GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) is a widely used benchmark of 8.5K grade-school math word problems designed to evaluate multi-step numerical reasoning. Each problem requires decomposing a natural-language description into structured arithmetic steps, making it a standard testbed for assessing chain-of-thought reasoning ability.• AIME24 (Maxwell-Jia, 2024) consists of 30 competition-level problems from the 2024 American Invitational Mathematics Examination. These questions span algebra, geometry, number theory, and combinatorics, and require precise numeric answers with typically 1-3 digits, making the benchmark a compact but challenging evaluation of high-school Olympiadstyle reasoning.• AIME25 (math ai, 2025) provides 30 additional problems from the 2025 AIME exam, maintaining the same answer format and difficulty profile. Compared with AIME24, this benchmark includes more multi-phase derivations and intricate combinatorial constructions, offering a complementary stress test for mathematical robustness.• GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2023) is the most difficult split of the GPQA benchmark with 198 questions, featuring graduate-level multiple-choice questions written by domain experts in physics, biology, and chemistry. The dataset emphasizes conceptual depth, cross-disciplinary reasoning, and the ability to synthesize multi-step scientific arguments under rigorous distractor settings.• MedQA (Yang et al., 2024a) contains real medical licensing exam questions that assess biomedical knowledge, clinical reasoning, and diagnostic decision-making. Problems require integrating textual context with domain-specific medical understanding, making the benchmark a representative testbed for professional-level scientific reasoning.Commonsense Reasoning.• ARC-Easy (Clark et al., 2018b) consists of grade-school science questions from the AI2 Reasoning Challenge that test foundational factual knowledge and straightforward commonsense reasoning. As a simplified subset of ARC, it serves as a baseline measure of basic scientific understanding without requiring complex multi-step inference.• ARC-Challenge (Clark et al., 2018a) includes the most difficult items from the AI2 Reasoning Challenge. These questions are intentionally adversarial, requiring multi-hop reasoning, causal and counterfactual inference, and systematic elimination of distractor choices. Performance on ARC-Challenge is widely regarded as a strong indicator of robust commonsense reasoning capabilities.Code Generation.• MBPP-Plus (Liu et al., 2023) extends the original MBPP benchmark with broader input coverage, additional hidden test cases, and stricter execution-based evaluation. Each problem requires generating a self-contained Python function that satisfies a comprehensive unit-test suite, making the benchmark a robust measure of code synthesis reliability and correctness.• HumanEval-Plus (Liu et al., 2023) augments HumanEval with denser, more challenging test suites, significantly increasing the rigor of functional correctness evaluation. The benchmark emphasizes generalization beyond prompt examples and tests a model's ability to produce semantically precise, executable Python code under more demanding verification settings.

Implementation DetailsIn addition to the experimental setups described in the main paper, we provide additional implementation and evaluation details below.Software Backend All methods are implemented in Python using PyTorch and HuggingFace Transformers, with an optional vLLM backend for fast decoding and tensor-parallel inference. We use the official chat templates and special tokens such as <|im start|> and <|im end|>.Evaluation protocol. For all non-coding benchmarks, we report accuracy based on answer matching of the final answer after text normalization (lowercasing, trimming whitespace, and removing extraneous punctuation).For multiple-choice datasets (GPQA-Diamond, MedQA, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge), we first extract the model's final answer string and then compare it via exact match to the answer letter.For numeric problems (GSM8k, AIME24, AIME25), we evaluate correctness based on numeric equality: we extract the final predicted answer, parse both prediction and answer into numbers, and mark as correct only if the two values match. Predictions that fail numeric parsing are counted as incorrect.For code generation tasks (MBPP-Plus and HumanEval-Plus), we evaluate the code by executing unit tests. Specifically, we extract the predicted code from model's output, append the ground-truth tests provided by the benchmark, and execute the combined script in a sandboxed environment with a 10-second timeout. A sample is counted as correct if and only if all tests pass without runtime errors.

G. Additional Discussions on LatentMASExtension to Heterogeneous Agents. For simplicity and training-free purposes, we assume that all agents in LatentMAS share the same shape of transformer layers. To relax this assumption and support heterogeneous agents in practice, one can directly leverage prior studies on layer mapping and ensemble learning (Ainsworth et al., 2022;Wortsman et al., 2022) by introducing a trainable adapter to align and share latent representations across different models.In addition, a potential future direction is to adapt advanced post-training paradigms from text-based MAS to optimize LatentMAS 's latent collaboration protocols to unlock more effective multi-agent reasoning strategies.
H. Additional Related WorksLatent Reasoning in LLMs. Beyond explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, recent work has explored the continuous latent space of LLMs as an alternative reasoning medium (Hao et al., 2024;Chen et al., 2025b;Zhu et al., 2025), revealing that hidden states encode richer semantic structures than what discrete token generation can express (Zhang et al., 2025;Liu et al., 2024). Latent reasoning methods such as CoCoNut (Hao et al., 2024) and latent-space editing approaches (e.g., RepE (Zou et al., 2023), LoT (Fungwacharakorn et al., 2024)) demonstrate that manipulating internal representations can guide models to reason more coherently and improve controllability without explicit token-level rationales. Other works (Li et al., 2025a;Wang et al., 2025b;Shi et al., 2025) have also extended latent reasoning paradigms to vision-language models. These methods leverage the structure of hidden states to perform interventions, such as steering, editing, or optimizing latent trajectories, that shape downstream reasoning behavior while remaining agnostic to surface-level text. By operating directly in the continuous space, they can induce reasoning steps that would be difficult or inefficient to express (Zhang et al., 2025;Liu et al., 2024;Coda-Forno et al., 2025). Despite these benefits, existing techniques are confined to a single model's internal computations and do not consider interaction or coordination across multiple reasoning entities (Hao et al., 2024). On the other hand, LatentMAS extends latent reasoning to a multi-agent setting, enabling each agent to generate latent thoughts and propagate latent information to others. Our new framework shifts latent reasoning from an isolated capability of individual models to a system-level collaborative mechanism.
Agentic Model Collaboration.With increasing algorithmic advances, LLM-based MAS have been applied across diverse domains (Sagi & Rokach, 2018;Chen et al., 2025a;Yan et al., 2025), such as math and science reasoning (Pezeshkpour et al., 2024;Yue et al., 2024;Wang et al., 2025a), open-domain question answering (Fourney et al., 2024;Wu et al., 2025), and multi-modal GUI interaction (Zhang et al., 2024a;Ye et al., 2025b), demonstrating their versatility in complex real-world settings. sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Model collaboration emerges as the foundation of systemlevel intelligence in the era of Agentic AI (Acharya et al., 2025). Recent advances in multi-agent systems (MAS) (Wu et al., 2024;Hu et al., 2025) have catalyzed a paradigm shift from solitary, model-centric reasoning into a collabora-tive endeavor among multiple interacting models. Among these, large language model (LLM)-based MAS has been adopted across various downstream applications, including cooperative math and science reasoning (Pezeshkpour et al., 2024;Zhou et al., 2025), automated code generation (Yang et al., 2024b;Ding et al., 2025), and open-domain question answering (Jin et al., 2025;Li et al., 2025c;2026). Within LLM-based MAS, natural language or text generally serves as the lingua franca -the common medium that carries each agent's internal thoughts and enables communication across different agents (Guo et al., 2024).Beyond explicit text, several studies have explored the use of LLMs' continuous latent space as a new form of "model language," (Chen et al., 2025b) by either (i) leveraging hidden representations within transformers to enable single model's internal latent chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning (Hao et al., 2024;Zheng et al., 2025;Zhang et al., 2025), or (ii) employing KV caches or layer embeddings for information exchange across two models (Liu et al., 2024;Fu et al., 2025). However, a comprehensive model collaboration framework unifying both latent reasoning and latent communication remains unexplored. Moving one step forward, we aim to investigate:

sections.title: Can MAS achieve pure latent collaboration?
sections.text: To address this question, we introduce LatentMAS, an endto-end collaborative framework that operates entirely within the continuous latent space. Our core design integrates both internal latent thoughts generation and cross-agent latent working memory transfer. Inside each agent, reasoning unfolds through auto-regressive generation of last-layer hidden representations, capturing the model's ongoing internal thoughts without explicit decoding. Across agents, information is exchanged via shared latent working memory stored in layer-wise KV caches, capturing both the input context and newly generated latent thoughts. Overall, LatentMAS is completely training-free, enabling all agents to think and interact purely through their internal latent representations.Building on this framework design, LatentMAS is grounded on three foundational principles, which are substantiated through comprehensive theoretical and empirical analyses:• Reasoning Expressiveness: Hidden representations naturally encode model continuous thoughts, making each latent step more expressive than discrete tokens and capable of conveying richer semantic information.• Communication Fidelity: Latent working memory preserves input representations and latent thoughts, enabling lossless information transfer across agents.• Collaboration Complexity: LatentMAS exhibits higher collaborative expressiveness than text-based MAS with substantially lower inference complexity.The first two principles jointly underscore the advantage of LatentMAS by enabling richer latent reasoning and lossless latent communication. The last principle characterizes how latent collaboration reshapes the efficiency-expressiveness tradeoff, illustrating that LatentMAS enables scalable multiagent coordination with reduced computational overhead.To empirically assess the efficacy of LatentMAS, we conduct comprehensive evaluations on 9 benchmarks spanning math and science reasoning, commonsense understanding, and code generation (Figure 1). Across both sequential and hierarchical MAS settings, and over five different backbone models spanning the Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025) and Llama3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024) families, LatentMAS consistently outperforms advanced single-model and text-based MAS baselines by (i) improving accuracy by up to 14.6%, (ii) reducing output token usage by 70.8%-83.7%, and (iii) delivering 4×-4.3× faster end-to-end inference. These results demonstrate that latent collaboration not only enhances system-level reasoning quality but also provides consistent efficiency gains without any additional training. Further detailed analyses of latent thought expressiveness, workingmemory transfer, and input-output alignment confirm that LatentMAS enables semantically meaningful, lossless, and stable collaboration entirely in latent space.

sections.title: Preliminary and Notations
sections.text: Auto-regressive Generation in Transformer. Let f θ (•) denotes the function computed by a standard Transformer model (Vaswani et al., 2017), parameterized by θ. Given an input sequence x = (x 1 , x 2 , . . . , x T ), the transformer f θ (•) first encodes each token via its input embedding layer W in to obtain token embeddings up to step t, i.e., E = [e 1 , e 2 , . . . , e t ] ∈ R t×d h , where d h is the model's hidden dimension. The input token embeddings E then successively process through L transformer layers in the forward pass through the model's residual stream, yielding the finallayer hidden representations H = [h 1 , h 2 , . . . , h t ] ∈ R t×d h . For next token generation, the model computes:f θ (x t+1 | x ≤t ) = softmax(h t W out ),(1)where W out denotes the language model head that maps the hidden representation to the vocabulary space. Each token is generated in an auto-regressive manner and appended to the input sequence. For latent generation, the model performs auto-regression over hidden representations instead of tokens, bypassing explicit decoding (Hao et al., 2024).

sections.title: KV Cache as Working Memory.
sections.text: In decoder-only Transformers, the Key-Value (KV) cache functions as a dynamic working memory during auto-regressive generation, storing intermediate representations from previous decoding steps to avoid redundant computation. Specifically, given the input embeddings E, each transformer layer projects them through projection matrices W Q , W K , W V to obtain Q, K, V . When the next token at step t + 1 is generated, the model appends its embedding to the input sequence and updates the cache (K cache , V cache ) as:K cache ← [K ≤t ; K t+1 ], V cache ← [V ≤t ; V t+1 ], (2)where K ≤t , V ≤t are accumulated key/value matrices from all previous steps and K t+1 , V t+1 are new key/value vectors computed from the current token's hidden state. This accumulative property enables the KV cache to maintain a growing working memory of model internal representations.

sections.title: LLM-based MAS Setting.
sections.text: We consider a multi-agent system S composed of N agents, denoted as A = {A 1 , A 2 , . . . , A N }, where each agent A i is an LLM corresponding to f θi above. At inference time, an input question q is provided to the system S, which orchestrates interactions among agents to collaboratively produce a final answer a corresponding to q. As MAS design paradigms are not definitive in general and often vary across downstream tasks (Tran et al., 2025;Cemri et al., 2025), we do not restrict our latent collaboration design to any particular architecture. Instead, we adopt two most commonly used MAS settings (sequential and hierarchical) as the bases to experimentally evaluate our method. Figure 2 illustrates the two MAS architecture settings. In the sequential MAS, we adopt a chain-of-agents design (Zhang et al., 2024b;Zhao et al., 2026) comprising four LLM agents: planner, critic, refiner, and solver. These agents assume complementary reasoning roles and are organized in a sequential pipeline, where the CoT output of each agent with the question q serves as the input to the next agent. In the hierarchical MAS, we adopt a domain-specialized design (Zhuge et al., 2024;Zhao et al., 2025). Multiple LLM agents, including code, math, and science agents, operate as different domain experts. Each agent independently reasons over the question q from its disciplinary perspective.A summarizer agent then receives all intermediate responses along with the question q and performs hierarchical aggregation to synthesize and refine the final answer.

sections.title: LatentMAS
sections.text: We introduce LatentMAS, an end-to-end latent collaboration framework that all agents reason and communicate entirely within the latent space. As illustrated in Figure 3, our method enables LLM agents to (i) auto-regressively generate expressive latent thoughts (Section 3.1), (ii) transfer latent working memory across agents with lossless communication fidelity (Section 3.2), and (iii) achieve lower inference complexity than text-based MAS while supporting a higher degree of model coordination (Section 3.3).

sections.title: Method Roadmap.
sections.text: In the following sub-sections, we present the complete pipeline of LatentMAS, detailing each component and interleaving theoretical analyses to justify the corresponding design principles.

sections.title: Auto-regressive Latent Thoughts Generation
sections.text: We first describe how each LLM agent performs latent reasoning through its layer-wise hidden states. Instead of decoding explicit tokens, reasoning unfolds directly within the agent by auto-regressively appending hidden representations from the final model layer.Given the input embeddings E = [e 1 , e 2 , . . . , e t ] containing the information from the question q and each agent's instruction prompt, each LLM agent A i ∈ A passes E through L transformer layers to compute the last-layer hidden representation h t at current step t. Then, we insert h t as the input embedding for the next step t + 1, replacing the original decoding and next-token embedding processes used in standard token generation. We auto-regressively repeat the process for m latent steps, yielding a sequence of newly generated last-layer hidden states H = [h t+1 , h t+2 , . . . , h t+m ].We define the continuous output representations H as the latent thoughts generated by A i .

sections.title: Input-Output Distribution Alignment.
sections.text: Since the newly generated H form a sequence of dense, high-level representations, directly inserting them into shallow layers as input embeddings may lead to out-of-distribution activations (Meegahapola et al., 2019;Zhou et al., 2019) , as these hidden states differ from the statistical patterns of learned token embeddings. To mitigate this in a training-free manner, we propose a linear alignment operator that maps last-layer hidden states back to the valid input embeddings. Specifically, given W in , W out as the input and output embedding layers of A i , we seek a projection matrix W a ∈ R d h ×d h that maps each output vector h ∈ H to a new input vector e to align with valid input space defined by W in :e = hW a , where W a ≈ W † out W in .(3)Here, W † out is the pseudo-inverse (Hoerl & Kennard, 1970) of W out (in Appendix A, we provide a detailed theoretical justification for the effectiveness of W a in the input-output alignment process, followed by a formal derivation of W a ).We then append the aligned vector e into the input sequence for auto-regressive latent generation. Note that W a is a small projection matrix of size d h × d h (e.g., d h =1024 for Qwen3-0.6B) and is computed once and reused in all subsequent latent steps. This design makes the alignment computationally negligible while maintaining distributional consistency between latent and discrete representations.Expressiveness on Continuous Latent Thoughts. With the mechanism of latent thought generation established within each agent, we next provide a theoretical analysis to quantify its representational advantage over conventional discrete token generation. The following theorem formalizes that latent thoughts, which inherently preserve richer semantic structures, achieve substantially higher expressive capacity than discrete text-based reasoning.Theorem 3.1 (Expressiveness of Latent Thoughts). Under the Linear Representation Hypothesis on h (stated in Assumption B.1), if the sequence of all latent thoughts with length m can be expressed losslessly through corresponding text-based reasoning, then the length of text (in tokens) needs to be at least Ω d h m/ log |V| , where |V| > 1 denotes the vocabulary size. Remark 3.2. Theorem 3.1 suggests that latent thoughts generation can be O d h / log |V| times more efficient than text-based reasoning. In addition, the expressiveness scales linearly with d h , implying that larger models inherently exhibits greater latent reasoning capacity.As an illustration to Remark 3.2, for Qwen3-4B / 8B / 14B models (Yang et al., 2025), latent thoughts generation can be 235.7 / 377.1 / 471.4 times more efficient than text-based reasoning. The full proof of Theorem 3.1 is provided in Appendix B.1. Beyond reasoning within individual agents, collaboration in LatentMAS further relies on how these agents exchange latent information, which we detail next.

sections.title: Thoughts Transfer via Latent Working Memory
sections.text: In text-based MAS, after one LLM agent completes its generation, the natural language output is directly appended to the input sequence of the next agent. However, since each agent in LatentMAS performs hidden-state generation without explicit text outputs, we design a new latent working memory transfer mechanism to ensure lossless information preservation and exchange.For clarity, we describe the memory transfer mechanism using the first two consecutive LLM agents A 1 , A 2 ∈ A.As shown in Figure 3, agent A 1 first performs m latent steps of generation (Section 3.1). After completing these steps, we extract the KV-caches from all L transformer layers of A 1 once and collect the latent working memory of A 1 as:M A1 = K (l) A1,cache , V(l)A1,cache l = 1, 2, . . . , L , with K (l) A1,cache = [K (l) A1,1 , . . . , K (l) A1,t+m ], and V (l) A1,cache = [V (l) A1,1 , . . . , V (l) A1,t+m ].(4) Here K (l) A1,cache and V (l)A1,cache are accumulated key and value matrices at the l-th layer. Unlike direct cache-sharing methods that exchange information mainly on prefilled input context across models, the collection of layer-wise caches in M A1 encapsulates both the initial input context and the newly generated latent thoughts of agent A 1 .Next, the successive agent A 2 integrates the working memory M A1 from agent A 1 . Before A 2 generates latent thoughts (i.e., last-layer hidden states), we perform layerwise concatenation to update its KV cache by prepending each K(l) A1,cache and V (l) A1,cache to existing K (l) A2,cache and V (l)A2,cache . By doing so, the new latent thoughts generation in A 2 is conditioned on both the working memory of A 1 and its own internal representations.

sections.title: Lossless Information Transfer.
sections.text: The latent working memory transfer mechanism ensures that each succeeding agent in LatentMAS seamlessly receives its predecessor's complete output without re-encoding. In the following theorem, we further formalize this property to demonstrate that latent working memory transfer guarantees information fidelity equivalent to explicit input exchange.

sections.title: Theorem 3.3 (Information Preservation via Latent Working Memory).
sections.text: In both latent and text-based reasoning, the outputs of an agent when receiving latent working memory from preceding agents are equivalent to those obtained when directly inputting the preceding agents' outputs.Full proof of Theorem 3.3 is provided in B.2. With lossless information preservation, we transfer latent working memory in KV rather than directly transmitting hidden states to avoid redundant recomputation for the successive agent.

sections.title: End-to-End Pipeline with Complexity Analyses
sections.text: For the remaining agents in LatentMAS, we follow the same latent thoughts generation and working memory transfer mechanism described above. Specifically, agent A 3 inherits the working memory M A2 from the preceding agent A 2 , performs auto-regressive last-layer hidden state generation, and subsequently transmits its updated latent working memory M A3 to the next agent. This process continues across all agents in LatentMAS, with only the last agent decoding the final answer in texts. In the following theorem, we theoretically analyze the overall complexity of LatentMAS.

sections.title: Theorem 3.4 (LatentMAS Complexity).
sections.text: The time complexity for each agent of LatentMAS is O (d 2 h m + d h m 2 + d h tm)L , where t is the input length of this agent, and m is the length of latent thoughts. In contrast, assuming Theorem 3.1, the time complexity for each agent of the vanilla text-based MAS needs to be O d3 h m 1 log |V| + d 3 h m 2 1 log 2 |V| + d 2 h tm 1 log |V| L + d 2 h |V|m 1 log |V|to achieve the same expressiveness.The full proof of Theorem 3.4 is provided in B.3. It is worth noting that LatentMAS is agnostic to specific model collaboration strategies and can be seamlessly applied to sequential, hierarchical, or other advanced MAS designs.

sections.text: Tasks and Datasets. We conduct comprehensive evaluations of LatentMAS across 9 benchmarks spanning both general-purpose and reasoning-intensive tasks: (i) Math & Science Reasoning, including GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), AIME24 (Maxwell-Jia, 2024), AIME25 (math ai, 2025), GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2023), and MedQA (Yang et al., 2024a); (ii) Commonsense Reasoning, including ARC-Easy (Clark et al., 2018b) and ARC-Challenge (Clark et al., 2018a); and (iii) Code Generation, including MBPP-Plus (Liu et al., 2023) and HumanEval-Plus (Liu et al., 2023). sections.title: Main Results
sections.text: Tables 1, 2, and 3 report the overall performance of Latent-MAS across 9 general and reasoning-intensive benchmarks built from 5 different scales of LLM backbones. To thoroughly examine collaboration behaviors during inference, we evaluate each method from three complementary perspectives: (i) task accuracy, (ii) system throughput (total output tokens), and (iii) end-to-end inference speed. Across all tasks, LatentMAS consistently improves over the singlemodel baseline by an average of 14.6% and 13.3% under the sequential and hierarchical settings, respectively, and further yields gains of 2.8% and 4.6% over text-based MAS. Under identical MAS architectures, LatentMAS provides 4× and 4.3× faster inference speed on average compared with sequential and hierarchical text-based MAS. Additionally, as the agents' collaboration occurs entirely in latent space, LatentMAS reduces token usage by 70.8% and 83.7% relative to sequential and hierarchical TextMAS. We leave additional results on Llama backbones in Appendix D.2. End-to-end Inference Speed. As established earlier in Theorem 3.1, LatentMAS can achieve orders-of-magnitude higher expressiveness, thereby enabling more efficient inference than text-based MAS. We further empirically validate this advantage through comparisons with TextMAS. As shown in Figure 4 and 10 (left), even after accelerating the TextMAS baselines using the vLLM service, LatentMAS still achieves a 2.6×-7× speedup over the vLLM-optimized TextMAS. This improvement stems from the substantially reduced number of latent steps required for latent thoughts generation compared with the much larger decoding steps needed for per-token text generation. With fewer than 50 latent steps, LatentMAS attains comparable or even higher performance on reasoning-intensive tasks such as AIME 24/25, whereas TextMAS typically requires more than 20K output tokens to complete full text-based CoT trajectories.Token Throughput. In addition, as illustrated in Figure 4 and 10 (right), LatentMAS reduces token usage by 59.4%-87.9% compared with TextMAS, as agents in LatentMAS communicate by directly transferring latent working memory into another agent's internal layers rather than relying on the text medium. LatentMAS also achieves 15.0%-60.3% lower token usage than single agents. Compared with singlemodel reasoning, LatentMAS distributes the input question across collaborating agents, greatly reducing the burden on the final agent, which primarily aggregates preceding latent thoughts and decodes the final answer using only a small number of tokens. As a result, the entire system generates fewer output tokens while still achieving higher accuracy.

sections.title: In-depth Analyses on LatentMAS
sections.text: Do Latent Thoughts Reflect Text Reasoning? We first verify whether latent thoughts generation in LatentMAS produces meaningful and semantically expressive representations. To this end, we compare the distribution of newly generated last-layer embeddings in LatentMAS with the embeddings of token-by-token responses produced by TextMAS.Experiments are conducted on 300 MedQA questions, using 40 latent steps for LatentMAS and a 4096 max-token budget for the TextMAS baseline.As shown in Figure 5, we highlight two key observations: (i) The last-layer embeddings from LatentMAS share nearly the same region of the embedding space with the token embeddings from TextMAS, indicating that latent thoughts encode similar semantic representations as the correct textQwen3-4B Qwen3-8B Qwen3-14B ℎ ! (ii) The last-layer embeddings from LatentMAS largely cover the distribution of token embeddings from TextMAS, indicating that latent thoughts offer greater diversity and expressive capacity than discrete tokens. Together, these findings show that latent thoughts not only capture the valid semantics of their corresponding text responses but also encode richer and more expressive representations inside. We further include a case study in Appendix J analyzing how LLM agents in LatentMAS interpret their own latent thoughts to provide additional validation.Effectiveness on Input-Output Alignment. We next empirically evaluate the effectiveness of the input-output alignment in our method design. First, we compare the input vector e t obtained from the standard token embedding layer with both the newly generated output vector h t before alignment and the after-aligned vector e t+1 . As shown in Figure 6, we visualize the three embedding vectors by comparing both density distributions and geometric relationships in the projected embedding space. We observe that the new h t deviates largely from the original input embedding e t .After applying W a , the aligned vector e t+1 realigns with e t , indicating that W a effectively restores the geometric and statistical structure of the input embedding space and mitigates representation drift across iterative latent steps.In Figure 7, across 3 different tasks, we further compare downstream performance before and after applying W a and observe consistent accuracy gains of 2.3%-5.3% by W a .

sections.title: Optimal Latent Step Depth.
sections.text: To understand how many latent steps are needed for optimal performance in Latent-MAS, we analyze the effect of increasing latent step depth across three downstream tasks. As shown in Figure 8, increasing the number of latent steps generally improves downstream performance, indicating that additional latent thoughts enhance collaborative expressiveness. Across the three tasks on Qwen3-14B, we find that accuracy steadily rises and peaks around 40-80 steps. Beyond this range, performance plateaus or declines, suggesting that excessive latent thought generation may introduce redundant or less useful information. Based on this observation, we adopt a moderate latent step budget within this range in practice, as it consistently provides the best accuracy-efficiency tradeoff without requiring any task-specific training procedures.

sections.title: Intermediate Error Tracking within LatentMAS.
sections.text: To better audit and interpret the latent collaboration process, we extend our original framework with an additional "debug mode" to enable a flexible conversion between inner latent thoughts and outer human-readable texts within each agent. We leave implementation details on how to converse to the debug mode in LatentMAS, together with additional detailed analyses and case studies, to Appendix E,F, and J.

sections.title: Related Work
sections.text: LLM-based Multi-agent Systems. Recent studies in Agentic AI have extended classical multi-agent systems (Hong et al., 2023;Park et al., 2023a;Yang et al., 2024c) grounded in traditional reinforcement learning and policy coordination, to modern LLM settings (Li et al., 2025b;Tan et al., 2025), enabling models to operate as autonomous agents that collaborate in reasoning, planning, and problemsolving (Tao et al., 2024;Wang et al., 2025c;Zhao et al., 2025). Early methods (Yao et al., 2022;Wu et al., 2024;Li et al., 2023) coordinate multiple LLMs through explicit dialogue and role assignment. Additional methods introduce structured communication protocols to enhance cooperation efficiency (Ye et al., 2025a) and emergent specialization (Mieczkowski et al., 2025;Huang et al., 2026) among agents. Building upon these advanced text-MAS methods, our work aims to construct a multi-agent collaboration system entirely in latent space, treating agents as tightly integrated components to achieve more expressive and efficient coordination.

sections.title: Model Collaboration in Latent Space.
sections.text: Recent studies on model collaboration (Tran et al., 2025) have gradually shifted from text-level coordination toward interaction directly in latent representations. Instead of exchanging information through texts, these works (Coda-Forno et al., 2025;Ye et al., 2025a;Fu et al., 2025;Zheng et al., 2025) enable models to communicate through model internal states such as hidden representations (Coda-Forno et al., 2025) for efficiency (Kong et al., 2026). Most existing methods rely on auxiliary alignment mechanisms and typically require additional training to facilitate effective cross-model communication. On the other hand, LatentMAS is a training-free latent multi-agent system in which each agent reasons and communicates via native latent representations.We leave additional related works on latent reasoning and agent collaboration in Appendix H.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: We introduce LatentMAS, a training-free framework that enables multi-agent systems to collaborate entirely within latent space. Our framework enables latent auto-regressive reasoning with a lossless latent working-memory transfer mechanism. Theoretical analyses and empirical evaluations across diverse reasoning and generation benchmarks demonstrate that LatentMAS consistently improves accuracy performance, token usage, and decoding speed over strong single-model and text-based MAS baselines. sections.title: C.1. Evaluation Details
sections.text: We introduce all datasets used in our experiments as follows:Math & Science Reasoning.• GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) is a widely used benchmark of 8.5K grade-school math word problems designed to evaluate multi-step numerical reasoning. Each problem requires decomposing a natural-language description into structured arithmetic steps, making it a standard testbed for assessing chain-of-thought reasoning ability.• AIME24 (Maxwell-Jia, 2024) consists of 30 competition-level problems from the 2024 American Invitational Mathematics Examination. These questions span algebra, geometry, number theory, and combinatorics, and require precise numeric answers with typically 1-3 digits, making the benchmark a compact but challenging evaluation of high-school Olympiadstyle reasoning.• AIME25 (math ai, 2025) provides 30 additional problems from the 2025 AIME exam, maintaining the same answer format and difficulty profile. Compared with AIME24, this benchmark includes more multi-phase derivations and intricate combinatorial constructions, offering a complementary stress test for mathematical robustness.• GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2023) is the most difficult split of the GPQA benchmark with 198 questions, featuring graduate-level multiple-choice questions written by domain experts in physics, biology, and chemistry. The dataset emphasizes conceptual depth, cross-disciplinary reasoning, and the ability to synthesize multi-step scientific arguments under rigorous distractor settings.• MedQA (Yang et al., 2024a) contains real medical licensing exam questions that assess biomedical knowledge, clinical reasoning, and diagnostic decision-making. Problems require integrating textual context with domain-specific medical understanding, making the benchmark a representative testbed for professional-level scientific reasoning.Commonsense Reasoning.• ARC-Easy (Clark et al., 2018b) consists of grade-school science questions from the AI2 Reasoning Challenge that test foundational factual knowledge and straightforward commonsense reasoning. As a simplified subset of ARC, it serves as a baseline measure of basic scientific understanding without requiring complex multi-step inference.• ARC-Challenge (Clark et al., 2018a) includes the most difficult items from the AI2 Reasoning Challenge. These questions are intentionally adversarial, requiring multi-hop reasoning, causal and counterfactual inference, and systematic elimination of distractor choices. Performance on ARC-Challenge is widely regarded as a strong indicator of robust commonsense reasoning capabilities.Code Generation.• MBPP-Plus (Liu et al., 2023) extends the original MBPP benchmark with broader input coverage, additional hidden test cases, and stricter execution-based evaluation. Each problem requires generating a self-contained Python function that satisfies a comprehensive unit-test suite, making the benchmark a robust measure of code synthesis reliability and correctness.• HumanEval-Plus (Liu et al., 2023) augments HumanEval with denser, more challenging test suites, significantly increasing the rigor of functional correctness evaluation. The benchmark emphasizes generalization beyond prompt examples and tests a model's ability to produce semantically precise, executable Python code under more demanding verification settings.

sections.title: C.2. Implementation Details
sections.text: In addition to the experimental setups described in the main paper, we provide additional implementation and evaluation details below.Software Backend All methods are implemented in Python using PyTorch and HuggingFace Transformers, with an optional vLLM backend for fast decoding and tensor-parallel inference. We use the official chat templates and special tokens such as <|im start|> and <|im end|>.Evaluation protocol. For all non-coding benchmarks, we report accuracy based on answer matching of the final answer after text normalization (lowercasing, trimming whitespace, and removing extraneous punctuation).For multiple-choice datasets (GPQA-Diamond, MedQA, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge), we first extract the model's final answer string and then compare it via exact match to the answer letter.For numeric problems (GSM8k, AIME24, AIME25), we evaluate correctness based on numeric equality: we extract the final predicted answer, parse both prediction and answer into numbers, and mark as correct only if the two values match. Predictions that fail numeric parsing are counted as incorrect.For code generation tasks (MBPP-Plus and HumanEval-Plus), we evaluate the code by executing unit tests. Specifically, we extract the predicted code from model's output, append the ground-truth tests provided by the benchmark, and execute the combined script in a sandboxed environment with a 10-second timeout. A sample is counted as correct if and only if all tests pass without runtime errors.

E.2. Quantifying Latent Thought Diversity.
sections.text: While Figure 5 provides a qualitative visualization of the embedding distributions, we further quantify the representational diversity of latent thoughts using a cosine-similarity-based metric. Specifically, for each method, we compute the average pairwise cosine similarity among the generated embeddings. A lower value indicates that the representations are less collapsed and more dispersed in the embedding space, corresponding to higher representational diversity. As shown in Table 6, LatentMAS consistently achieves lower average cosine similarity than TextMAS across all three Qwen3 backbones. This confirms that the latent thoughts are not merely aligned with the semantic region of text-based reasoning but also span a broader and less concentrated representation space. Together with Figure 5, these results provide both qualitative and quantitative evidence that latent thoughts preserve semantic consistency with text reasoning while offering richer representational diversity.

sections.title: E.3. Ablations on Latent Reasoning and Communication in LatentMAS
sections.text: To isolate the contribution of each component in LatentMAS, we further conduct hybrid ablations by selectively replacing either latent reasoning or latent communication with its text-based counterpart. Specifically, we compare LatentMAS with the following two variants:• Latent Reasoning + Text Communication, where each agent performs latent reasoning but communicates to the next agent through decoded text, using only the last 128 decoded tokens;• Text Reasoning + Latent Communication, where each agent performs standard text-based reasoning while transferring intermediate information to the next agent through latent working memory.As shown in Table 7, both hybrid variants underperform full LatentMAS across all evaluated tasks. This demonstrates that the gains of LatentMAS cannot be attributed to only one component. Latent reasoning improves the expressiveness of each agent's internal computation, while latent communication preserves and transfers intermediate information without forcing it through a compressed text interface. Combining both components enables end-to-end latent collaboration and yields the strongest performance.Table 7. Hybrid ablations on latent reasoning and latent communication using Qwen3-8B. Replacing either component with its text-based counterpart leads to consistent performance drops, indicating that both components contribute to the overall gains of LatentMAS.

How to Debug LatentMAS?In LatentMAS "debug mode", we introduce a switch that enables us to inspect the content of the latent thoughts of agents without altering the overall LatentMAS pipeline. Specifically, when we switch on the "debug mode", each agent should simultaneously generate its latent thoughts and another text response within the same contextual information (e.g., agent prompt and latent working memory). The latent thoughts are passed to the next agent, and the parallel text response serves as a probe for the latent thoughts.By checking the details of text response of intermediate agents, we can identify the root causes of errors in the final answer.To illustrate this, we present two distinct case studies generated in "debug mode" using Qwen3-14B model on GSM8K dataset, corresponding to a failure case and a success case below.• Case 1: Incorrect Intermediate Text Leads to Error in LatentMAS Answer. In the first case of Section I, we examine a problem where LatentMAS produces an incorrect final answer. According to the intermediate agent output, we find the Refiner agent gives an incorrect numerical relationship (as highlighted in red), leading the final Solver agent to utilize this erroneous dependency in its calculation.• Case 2: Correct Intermediate Text Leads to Correct LatentMAS Answer. Conversely, in the second case of Section I, all intermediate agents produce logically sound intermediate outputs, which successfully guides the final agent to derive the correct answer.Finally, to quantitatively validate that the text in "debug mode" serves as a faithful probe for LatentMAS, we conduct a correlation study on 100 debug text -final answer pairs using Qwen3-14B model on GSM8K dataset, which consists of 80 instances with correct final answers and 20 instances with incorrect final answers. We manually annotated the correctness of the each debug text and analyzed their correlation with the final correctness of LatentMAS. As shown in Table 8, we observe a high consistency between the correctness of the intermediate text and the final answer. We find that 96.2% of the intermediate text are valid when the final answer is correct, while 90.0% contain errors when the final answer contains error. The result shows that the correctness of intermediate text output aligns well with LatentMAS, validating the "debug mode" as a reliable probe for our framework.

sections.title: G. Additional Discussions on LatentMAS
sections.text: Extension to Heterogeneous Agents. For simplicity and training-free purposes, we assume that all agents in LatentMAS share the same shape of transformer layers. To relax this assumption and support heterogeneous agents in practice, one can directly leverage prior studies on layer mapping and ensemble learning (Ainsworth et al., 2022;Wortsman et al., 2022) by introducing a trainable adapter to align and share latent representations across different models.In addition, a potential future direction is to adapt advanced post-training paradigms from text-based MAS to optimize LatentMAS 's latent collaboration protocols to unlock more effective multi-agent reasoning strategies.

sections.title: H. Additional Related Works
sections.text: Latent Reasoning in LLMs. Beyond explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, recent work has explored the continuous latent space of LLMs as an alternative reasoning medium (Hao et al., 2024;Chen et al., 2025b;Zhu et al., 2025), revealing that hidden states encode richer semantic structures than what discrete token generation can express (Zhang et al., 2025;Liu et al., 2024). Latent reasoning methods such as CoCoNut (Hao et al., 2024) and latent-space editing approaches (e.g., RepE (Zou et al., 2023), LoT (Fungwacharakorn et al., 2024)) demonstrate that manipulating internal representations can guide models to reason more coherently and improve controllability without explicit token-level rationales. Other works (Li et al., 2025a;Wang et al., 2025b;Shi et al., 2025) have also extended latent reasoning paradigms to vision-language models. These methods leverage the structure of hidden states to perform interventions, such as steering, editing, or optimizing latent trajectories, that shape downstream reasoning behavior while remaining agnostic to surface-level text. By operating directly in the continuous space, they can induce reasoning steps that would be difficult or inefficient to express (Zhang et al., 2025;Liu et al., 2024;Coda-Forno et al., 2025). Despite these benefits, existing techniques are confined to a single model's internal computations and do not consider interaction or coordination across multiple reasoning entities (Hao et al., 2024). On the other hand, LatentMAS extends latent reasoning to a multi-agent setting, enabling each agent to generate latent thoughts and propagate latent information to others. Our new framework shifts latent reasoning from an isolated capability of individual models to a system-level collaborative mechanism.
